subtopics.title: divisibility
subtopics.teaching: Divisibility problems use exact integer structure: if a divides b, then b is an integer multiple of a. Factorization, divisibility tests and modular reasoning help expose hidden structure.
subtopics.worked_example: To test whether 3 divides 4,872, add its digits: 4+8+7+2=21, which is divisible by 3, so 4,872 is divisible by 3.
subtopics.pitfall: A divisibility test is not interchangeable with another test; the digit-sum rule for 3 does not prove divisibility by 8.
subtopics.mastery: Use divisibility rules and factor structure to solve unfamiliar integer problems and justify each step.

subtopics.title: remainders
subtopics.teaching: Remainder arithmetic studies what remains after division and can simplify large-number problems by working modulo a convenient integer.
subtopics.worked_example: For the last digit of 7^n, work modulo 10 and observe the repeating cycle 7, 9, 3, 1.
subtopics.pitfall: Reducing a number modulo m does not mean replacing it with an unrelated value; operations must respect modular equivalence.
subtopics.mastery: Choose an appropriate modulus, identify cycles, and calculate remainders without expanding unnecessarily large powers.

subtopics.title: prime structures
subtopics.teaching: Prime numbers are integers greater than 1 with exactly two positive divisors. Prime factorization provides a canonical way to analyze divisibility, gcd, lcm and divisor counts.
subtopics.worked_example: The factorization 360=2^3×3^2×5 reveals its divisor structure and makes related questions easier.
subtopics.pitfall: Treating 1 as prime or assuming every composite number has only two factors leads to structural errors.
subtopics.mastery: Factor integers into primes and use exponents to derive divisor and divisibility properties.

subtopics.title: gcd and lcm
subtopics.teaching: The greatest common divisor captures the largest shared factor, while the least common multiple captures the smallest positive shared multiple. Prime exponents give a systematic method for both.
subtopics.worked_example: For 84=2^2×3×7 and 126=2×3^2×7, the gcd uses minimum exponents and the lcm uses maximum exponents.
subtopics.pitfall: Using maximum exponents for gcd or minimum exponents for lcm reverses the underlying rule.
subtopics.mastery: Compute gcd and lcm efficiently and apply them to scheduling, grouping and integer-structure problems.

subtopics.title: number patterns
subtopics.teaching: Number patterns can arise from arithmetic relationships, modular cycles, factor structure, recursive rules or digit operations. The goal is to identify a rule that explains all supplied terms.
subtopics.worked_example: For 2, 5, 10, 17, 26, the differences are 3, 5, 7, 9, suggesting n²+1 for the nth term.
subtopics.pitfall: Matching only the first two or three terms can support many false rules.
subtopics.mastery: Test a proposed pattern against multiple terms and derive a rule that can be justified rather than guessed.

subtopics.title: fractions and ratios
subtopics.teaching: Fractions represent quantities as a ratio of integers, while ratios compare quantities using consistent units. Competition problems often require scaling, simplification and equivalent representations.
subtopics.worked_example: If 3/5 of a quantity is 24, multiply by 5/3 to recover the whole quantity: 40.
subtopics.pitfall: Adding numerators and denominators separately does not generally preserve fraction equivalence.
subtopics.mastery: Move confidently among fractions, ratios and whole quantities while tracking units and scale factors.

subtopics.title: percentages
subtopics.teaching: Percentage problems describe relative change using a base quantity. Successive percentage changes must be applied to the updated value rather than simply added.
subtopics.worked_example: A 20% increase followed by a 20% decrease multiplies a quantity by 1.2×0.8=0.96, producing a net 4% decrease.
subtopics.pitfall: A percentage change is meaningless without identifying the quantity used as the base.
subtopics.mastery: Solve successive-change and reverse-percentage problems by explicitly identifying the base amount.

subtopics.title: rates
subtopics.teaching: A rate compares quantities measured in different units, such as distance per time, work per hour or cost per item. Unit consistency is essential.
subtopics.worked_example: If a cyclist travels 36 km in 2 hours, the average speed is 18 km/h; converting minutes or seconds incorrectly would change the result.
subtopics.pitfall: Adding rates from different tasks without considering how the tasks combine can produce incorrect answers.
subtopics.mastery: Set up rate equations with consistent units and distinguish average rate from component rates.

subtopics.title: proportional reasoning
subtopics.teaching: Direct proportion means one quantity changes by a constant factor with another, while inverse proportion means their product remains constant under stated conditions.
subtopics.worked_example: If four identical machines complete a fixed job in 6 hours under ideal assumptions, doubling the machines suggests half the time: 3 hours.
subtopics.pitfall: Not every relationship that increases together is directly proportional.
subtopics.mastery: Identify the relationship type, state its assumptions and use scaling factors correctly.

subtopics.title: integer problems
subtopics.teaching: Integer problems use whole-number constraints, signs, parity, divisibility and bounds. The discrete nature of integers often provides stronger restrictions than continuous algebra alone.
subtopics.worked_example: If two integers have an odd sum, one must be even and the other odd, because equal parity would produce an even sum.
subtopics.pitfall: Solving an integer problem over all real numbers can produce answers that violate the original domain.
subtopics.mastery: Use parity, bounds, divisibility and integer constraints to eliminate impossible cases.

subtopics.title: expressions
subtopics.teaching: Algebraic expressions combine constants, variables and operations according to a precise order and structure. Simplification preserves value while revealing useful forms.
subtopics.worked_example: Expanding (x+3)(x+5) gives x²+8x+15, which can then be compared with other expressions.
subtopics.pitfall: Combining unlike terms such as x and x² as though they were the same changes the expression.
subtopics.mastery: Simplify, expand and factor expressions accurately and explain why each transformation preserves value.

subtopics.title: equations
subtopics.teaching: An equation asserts equality between two expressions. Solving means finding values that satisfy the equality while respecting restrictions introduced by operations.
subtopics.worked_example: For 3x+5=20, subtract 5 and divide by 3 to obtain x=5, then substitute back to verify.
subtopics.pitfall: Multiplying or dividing by an expression that could be zero can introduce or lose solutions if restrictions are ignored.
subtopics.mastery: Solve equations systematically, state domain restrictions and verify candidate solutions.

subtopics.title: inequalities
subtopics.teaching: Inequalities compare quantities and describe sets of possible values rather than usually one exact answer. Multiplying or dividing by a negative reverses the inequality sign.
subtopics.worked_example: From -2x>6, division by -2 gives x<-3, with the inequality direction reversed.
subtopics.pitfall: Solving an inequality like an equation without reversing the sign under a negative multiplier gives the wrong solution set.
subtopics.mastery: Solve linear and basic nonlinear inequalities and represent the resulting solution region correctly.

subtopics.title: identities
subtopics.teaching: An algebraic identity is true for every value in its stated domain, unlike an equation that may hold only for particular values. Standard identities can transform difficult expressions.
subtopics.worked_example: The identity (a+b)^2=a²+2ab+b² follows by expansion and holds for all real a and b.
subtopics.pitfall: Confusing an identity with a conditional equation can lead to incorrect assumptions about when it is valid.
subtopics.mastery: Recognize, prove and apply common algebraic identities in unfamiliar competition problems.

subtopics.title: algebraic problem solving
subtopics.teaching: Competition algebra often requires translating a verbal condition into variables, selecting a useful representation and combining several constraints before solving.
subtopics.worked_example: If a rectangle has perimeter 30 and length is twice its width, writing 2(2w+w)=30 reduces the problem to one variable.
subtopics.pitfall: Choosing variables without defining what they represent can produce equations that encode the wrong situation.
subtopics.mastery: Translate a multi-condition problem into algebra, solve it, and interpret the result in the original context.

subtopics.title: angles
subtopics.teaching: Angle relationships arise from lines, intersections, polygons and parallel-line configurations. Recognizing invariant relationships can reduce a diagram to a few equations.
subtopics.worked_example: If two adjacent angles form a straight line and one is 68°, the other is 112° because their sum is 180°.
subtopics.pitfall: A diagram drawn approximately is not proof that two angles are equal or lines are parallel.
subtopics.mastery: Use angle sums and parallel-line relationships to derive unknown angles from stated facts.

subtopics.title: triangles
subtopics.teaching: Triangles obey angle-sum and side relationships, including isosceles properties, congruence, similarity and the Pythagorean theorem in right triangles.
subtopics.worked_example: A right triangle with legs 6 and 8 has hypotenuse 10 by the Pythagorean theorem.
subtopics.pitfall: The Pythagorean theorem applies only to right triangles, and visual appearance is not enough to establish congruence.
subtopics.mastery: Select appropriate triangle theorems and justify the relationship before calculating.

subtopics.title: polygons
subtopics.teaching: For an n-sided polygon, the sum of interior angles is (n−2)×180°. Regular polygons add equal-angle and symmetry constraints.
subtopics.worked_example: A regular hexagon has interior-angle sum 720°, so each interior angle is 120°.
subtopics.pitfall: The interior-angle sum is not the measure of one angle in a regular polygon.
subtopics.mastery: Use polygon angle formulas and symmetry to solve multi-step geometry problems.

subtopics.title: circles
subtopics.teaching: Circle geometry uses radius, diameter, circumference, area, arcs, chords, tangents and angle relationships. The same radius and central-angle structure often unlocks competition problems.
subtopics.worked_example: A circle with radius 7 has circumference 14π and area 49π; the formulas use the same radius but describe different quantities.
subtopics.pitfall: Confusing circumference with area or radius with diameter creates systematic factor errors.
subtopics.mastery: Apply circle formulas and basic angle, chord and tangent relationships while tracking what each quantity represents.

subtopics.title: area and geometry proofs
subtopics.teaching: Area methods combine formulas, decomposition, rearrangement and sometimes similarity or algebra. Geometry proofs require a logically ordered chain from given facts to the desired conclusion.
subtopics.worked_example: A complex polygon can be split into rectangles and triangles, while a proof may establish equal areas by showing two triangles share a base and have equal heights.
subtopics.pitfall: A numerical diagram is not proof; measurements or visual symmetry cannot replace stated geometric reasons.
subtopics.mastery: Calculate composite areas and write short proofs in which every conclusion follows from a stated theorem, definition or given fact.

subtopics.title: counting principles
subtopics.teaching: Combinatorics begins by deciding whether choices are independent, sequential, grouped or overlapping. The multiplication principle counts successive choices, while the addition principle combines mutually exclusive cases.
subtopics.worked_example: If a meal has 3 starters and 4 main courses and one of each is chosen, there are 3×4=12 possible meals.
subtopics.pitfall: Multiplying counts that are not independent or adding cases that overlap can double-count outcomes.
subtopics.mastery: Choose and justify an addition or multiplication structure before calculating a total.

subtopics.title: arrangements
subtopics.teaching: Arrangements count ordered outcomes. Permutations are appropriate when position matters, while repeated or restricted elements require additional care.
subtopics.worked_example: Three distinct books can be arranged on a shelf in 3!=6 orders.
subtopics.pitfall: Treating an ordered arrangement as an unordered selection loses positional information.
subtopics.mastery: Determine whether order matters and count arrangements with repeated or restricted positions correctly.

subtopics.title: selections
subtopics.teaching: Selections count groups where order does not matter. Binomial coefficients provide a systematic method for choosing a fixed number from a larger set.
subtopics.worked_example: Choosing 2 students from 5 gives C(5,2)=10 groups because the pair {A,B} is the same selection as {B,A}.
subtopics.pitfall: Counting the same group in different orders creates duplicates.
subtopics.mastery: Distinguish combinations from permutations and solve selection problems with stated restrictions.

subtopics.title: casework
subtopics.teaching: Casework partitions a problem into distinct, exhaustive cases and solves each case without overlap. Good casework reduces complexity rather than multiplying possibilities blindly.
subtopics.worked_example: A digit problem can be split into cases based on whether the first digit is zero, even or odd, provided the cases are mutually exclusive and cover every allowed outcome.
subtopics.pitfall: Missing a case or allowing two cases to overlap causes an incorrect total.
subtopics.mastery: Design a complete, non-overlapping case split and combine the results accurately.

subtopics.title: inclusion exclusion basics
subtopics.teaching: Inclusion-exclusion corrects double counting when sets overlap. For two sets, the size of their union equals the sum of their sizes minus the intersection.
subtopics.worked_example: If 18 students like chess, 12 like coding and 5 like both, then 25 like at least one: 18+12−5.
subtopics.pitfall: Adding set sizes without subtracting the overlap counts shared members twice.
subtopics.mastery: Identify overlaps and apply inclusion-exclusion to small multi-set counting problems.

subtopics.title: arithmetic sequences
subtopics.teaching: An arithmetic sequence has a constant common difference. Its nth term is a+(n−1)d and its partial sum can be found from the first and last terms.
subtopics.worked_example: For 7, 11, 15, 19,... the common difference is 4, so the 10th term is 7+9×4=43.
subtopics.pitfall: Using the first term as though it were the zeroth term shifts the index and produces an off-by-one error.
subtopics.mastery: Find terms and sums of arithmetic sequences and translate between recursive and explicit descriptions.

subtopics.title: geometric sequences
subtopics.teaching: A geometric sequence has a constant common ratio. Its nth term scales multiplicatively rather than by a fixed difference.
subtopics.worked_example: For 3, 6, 12, 24,... the ratio is 2 and the 6th term is 3×2^5=96.
subtopics.pitfall: A constant difference does not imply a geometric sequence, and the ratio must be defined where division is valid.
subtopics.mastery: Identify common ratios and calculate terms or finite sums of geometric sequences.

subtopics.title: recurrences
subtopics.teaching: A recurrence defines terms from earlier terms. Solving or analyzing it requires tracking the initial conditions as well as the update rule.
subtopics.worked_example: The Fibonacci sequence uses a_n=a_(n−1)+a_(n−2) with initial terms 0 and 1; both the recurrence and starting values are necessary.
subtopics.pitfall: A recurrence without initial conditions may not determine a unique sequence.
subtopics.mastery: Generate terms accurately and reason from a recurrence while preserving its initial conditions.

subtopics.title: visual patterns
subtopics.teaching: Visual patterns encode numerical relationships through shapes, grids, tiles or growing arrangements. Translating the visual structure into a count often reveals a sequence or formula.
subtopics.worked_example: A row of joined squares may use one new edge-sharing square at each step, allowing the number of tiles or exposed sides to be expressed as a function of the step number.
subtopics.pitfall: Guessing from the first few drawings without identifying what changes between stages can lead to the wrong rule.
subtopics.mastery: Translate a visual growth rule into a numerical sequence or formula and justify the pattern.

subtopics.title: pattern proofs
subtopics.teaching: A pattern becomes mathematically reliable when the rule is justified rather than merely observed. Induction, algebraic derivation or structural reasoning can provide that justification.
subtopics.worked_example: To justify 1+3+5+...+(2n−1)=n², one can show the next odd number converts n² into (n+1)².
subtopics.pitfall: Checking many examples provides evidence but does not by itself prove a statement for every allowed n.
subtopics.mastery: Distinguish observation from proof and justify a general pattern using an appropriate method.

subtopics.title: sample spaces
subtopics.teaching: A sample space lists or characterizes all possible outcomes of a random experiment. Correct probability calculations depend on defining the relevant outcomes and their weights.
subtopics.worked_example: For one fair coin and one fair die, the sample space has 2×6=12 equally likely elementary outcomes.
subtopics.pitfall: Ignoring an outcome or treating unequal outcomes as equally likely can distort the probability.
subtopics.mastery: Define a complete sample space and determine whether its outcomes are equally likely before calculating.

subtopics.title: probability rules
subtopics.teaching: Probability values lie between 0 and 1. Complement, addition and multiplication rules allow compound events to be calculated when their relationships are understood.
subtopics.worked_example: For any event A, P(not A)=1−P(A). If two events are mutually exclusive, P(A or B)=P(A)+P(B).
subtopics.pitfall: Using the multiplication rule merely because two events occur in the same question ignores whether they are independent or conditional.
subtopics.mastery: Select the correct probability rule based on event relationships and justify its use.

subtopics.title: expected outcomes
subtopics.teaching: Expected value is the probability-weighted average of possible numerical outcomes. It describes long-run average behaviour, not a guaranteed result of one trial.
subtopics.worked_example: For a fair six-sided die, the expected roll is (1+2+3+4+5+6)/6=3.5 even though 3.5 cannot appear on one roll.
subtopics.pitfall: Expected value should not be interpreted as the outcome that must occur or even the most likely single outcome.
subtopics.mastery: Calculate and interpret expected values as long-run averages and distinguish them from actual outcomes.

subtopics.title: data analysis
subtopics.teaching: Data analysis involves organizing, summarizing and interpreting numerical information using measures such as mean, median, range and appropriate charts.
subtopics.worked_example: For 2, 3, 3, 8, 14, the median is 3 while the mean is 6, illustrating how an extreme value can pull the mean upward.
subtopics.pitfall: Averages can hide spread or skew, and a chart can mislead if its scale is distorted.
subtopics.mastery: Choose appropriate summaries and interpret center, spread and outliers rather than relying on one statistic.

subtopics.title: conditional reasoning
subtopics.teaching: Conditional probability measures the chance of an event given that another event is known to have occurred. The new information can change the relevant sample space.
subtopics.worked_example: If a card is known to be a face card, the probability it is a king is 4/12=1/3 because only the 12 face cards remain relevant.
subtopics.pitfall: Using the original sample space after receiving new information ignores the condition.
subtopics.mastery: Update the sample space or use P(A|B)=P(A and B)/P(B) to solve conditional problems.

subtopics.title: invariants
subtopics.teaching: An invariant is a quantity or property that remains unchanged under every allowed move of a process. It can prove that a target state is impossible even when many moves are possible.
subtopics.worked_example: If an operation always changes a number by an even amount, its parity remains invariant, so an odd starting value can never become even.
subtopics.pitfall: A quantity that changes during a move is not an invariant merely because it often looks similar.
subtopics.mastery: Identify a property preserved by every legal operation and use it to constrain reachable states.

subtopics.title: extremal reasoning
subtopics.teaching: Extremal reasoning focuses on a largest, smallest, earliest or otherwise extreme object because its properties can force constraints on the rest of a configuration.
subtopics.worked_example: In a finite set of integers, choosing the smallest counterexample can allow a proof to show that a still smaller counterexample must exist, producing a contradiction.
subtopics.pitfall: Selecting an arbitrary example instead of a genuinely extreme one removes the key logical leverage.
subtopics.mastery: Identify a useful extremal object and derive a contradiction or structural conclusion from its extremal property.

subtopics.title: working backwards
subtopics.teaching: Working backwards starts from the required final condition and reverses valid operations to recover possible starting states or necessary intermediate states.
subtopics.worked_example: If a number is doubled and then 5 is added to obtain 23, reverse the operations: 23−5=18 and 18÷2=9.
subtopics.pitfall: Reversing operations in the wrong order or ignoring non-reversible steps can create false solutions.
subtopics.mastery: Reverse a sequence of operations carefully and verify the recovered starting state by running the original process forward.

subtopics.title: construction
subtopics.teaching: Constructive problems ask for an explicit object satisfying given conditions rather than only proving that one exists. A successful construction must be checked against every constraint.
subtopics.worked_example: To show that a required arrangement exists, build a specific arrangement and verify each adjacency or counting condition.
subtopics.pitfall: Producing an example that satisfies most but not all constraints is not a valid construction.
subtopics.mastery: Build explicit examples systematically and verify every required condition.

subtopics.title: multi-step proofs
subtopics.teaching: Competition proofs often combine definitions, lemmas, algebraic transformations and contradiction or induction. Each step must follow from established facts.
subtopics.worked_example: A geometry proof might first establish two triangles are similar, then use corresponding ratios to derive the requested length.
subtopics.pitfall: Skipping the justification for a crucial intermediate claim can make a proof appear plausible while leaving a logical gap.
subtopics.mastery: Organize a multi-step proof into justified claims and ensure the conclusion follows from the chain of evidence.

subtopics.title: estimation
subtopics.teaching: Estimation provides a fast reasonableness check and can sometimes eliminate answer choices before exact calculation. It relies on controlled rounding and scale awareness.
subtopics.worked_example: To estimate 49.8×20.2, round to about 50×20=1000 before checking an exact result.
subtopics.pitfall: Rounding in inconsistent directions or too aggressively can produce an estimate that is not useful.
subtopics.mastery: Choose sensible approximations, estimate the scale of an answer and use the estimate to detect implausible results.

subtopics.title: time allocation
subtopics.teaching: Competition time management means allocating effort according to question difficulty, scoring value and remaining time rather than spending too long on one obstacle.
subtopics.worked_example: If a paper contains easy, medium and difficult questions, securing the easy marks first can leave more time for high-value problems later.
subtopics.pitfall: Spending most of the available time on the first difficult question can reduce the total score even if that question is eventually solved.
subtopics.mastery: Use a deliberate first pass, mark uncertain problems and redistribute time based on progress.

subtopics.title: answer verification
subtopics.teaching: Verification checks whether a solution satisfies the original conditions and whether arithmetic, units, signs and logical assumptions are consistent.
subtopics.worked_example: After solving x=5, substitute it into the original equation rather than checking only the transformed equation.
subtopics.pitfall: A calculation can be internally consistent yet answer a different question because of an incorrect interpretation.
subtopics.mastery: Substitute, estimate, inspect units and reread the original condition before finalizing an answer.

subtopics.title: error analysis
subtopics.teaching: Error analysis identifies where a solution first diverged from valid reasoning and distinguishes conceptual mistakes from arithmetic or transcription errors.
subtopics.worked_example: If a student applies the correct formula but substitutes the wrong value, the repair is different from choosing an invalid theorem in the first place.
subtopics.pitfall: Fixing only the final number without locating the first invalid step can leave the underlying misconception unchanged.
subtopics.mastery: Locate the first incorrect step, classify the error and state the correct reasoning that replaces it.

subtopics.title: mixed championship sets
subtopics.teaching: Mixed sets require switching among number theory, algebra, geometry, combinatorics, probability and proof without being told the topic in advance. The key skill is rapid problem classification.
subtopics.worked_example: A mixed paper may place a modular arithmetic problem beside a geometry proof; first identify the governing structure before selecting a method.
subtopics.pitfall: Continuing with the method used on the previous question can bias the solver toward the wrong mathematical tool.
subtopics.mastery: Classify unfamiliar problems quickly, select an appropriate strategy, solve rigorously and verify the result.
